Thomas.topographic_classification: Nearly Flat Tableland / High Plains Upland
Thomas.water_erosion_hazard: Very Low (insufficient slope velocity to generate sheet or rill erosion on upland flats)
Thomas.why_wind_drives_erosion: In Western Kansas tablelands, topography is exceptionally flat (< 1% slope). Water-driven runoff erosion is minimal on these uplands. Instead, soil erosion is almost entirely driven by HIGH WIND VELOCITIES. With no natural topographic barriers or timber breaks, sustained 30–50 mph spring winds generate severe shear stress at the ground surface. When summer fallow leaves silt-loam topsoil bare and pulverized, soil grains detach through saltation and suspension. Therefore, erosion control does not depend on contouring or terracing; it rests strictly on SOIL ARMOR (standing crop residue and living canopies) during high-wind months.

Finney.topographic_classification: Gently Undulating High Plains & Arkansas River Alluvial Terrace
Finney.water_erosion_hazard: Low (confined to localized breaks near Arkansas River drainage)
Finney.why_wind_drives_erosion: Finney County fields average less than 1% slope across broad center-pivot circles. Because slope steepness is negligible, water runoff does not drive topsoil loss. Erosion is overwhelmingly driven by WIND DETACHMENT. During dry winter and spring transitions, unprotected topsoil is subject to abrasive wind currents. Maintaining heavy corn and sorghum root structures and surface stover is the primary physical defense against wind-blown topsoil loss.
